utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did I understand you correctly that you wanted to address the Chamber this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence wanted to submit to the Registry this morning a motion based on the decision you issued on the 8th of April 2002. The decision was that every time there is a problem involving the quality of a document. We have informed the Prosecution about this move but we have been unable to submit this motion officially to the Registry with the appropriate stamps. We will do so during the first break because the personnel in charge of these tasks were still not at work. Mr. President, we wanted to present the views of the Defence before the Chamber for the following reasons: We know that this week we are not sitting on Friday. The documents in question relate to the witness who will be here tomorrow or on Monday at the latest and if we fail to receive from the Prosecution a clear view, a clear position, I hope that it will be clearer than some of the documents because sometimes we can't see anything. We will be unable to proceed. We will pinpoint the problem. We have been discussing this for some time now. But we could like the Chamber to request from the Prosecution all of the documents that we specified, for these documents to be submitted to us as quickly as possible. These documents, I believe that we can show them to you, Mr. President, but when we received such documents from the Prosecution, I believe it is not necessary for me to make any lengthy comments. I can show you other documents too, which, unlike these have been copied so many times that they look as if three pages have been copied onto the same page. You have the text from the left to the right, from the right to the left, and we are absolutely unable to read anything. It is a massacre. When I say that it is a massacre, I want to say that this is in fact a result of a hunt for the documents on the part of the Defence. And I want to know what we are talking about, what we are dealing with because we cannot do anything with such documents, Mr. President. That is why we would like the Prosecution to give us for all the numbers -- documents under the numbers that were listed yesterday, we informed them yesterday, last night for them documents to provide us with the clear and legible copies which would enable both the Trial Chamber and the Defence to work properly. So these are all the documents that are at their disposal. The last thing I wanted to say is that it is quite clear that nothing can be done about it. There are some documents that are more subtle, so to speak, where only one or two lines may be legible. We have seen it yesterday. A line was not translated and that line is important. That means that the person who actually wrote the document was, in fact, a member of a military institution, a military institution that His Excellency General Galic was fighting against. These documents were drafted in 1995 at the time when the hostilities were ongoing. Without this part, the text has a totally different impact, and for us, it is important to get the full information. For instance, Mr. President, the very fact that these documents may be compared to -- so that we can see whether everything has been translated, it takes quite a lot of time for us. It is a waste of time and effort for us. We cannot do so for every witness and before every hearing, we cannot spend three or four hours checking whether all the documents have been translated properly, whether the two versions correspond and so on and so forth. It seems that the goal is to exhaust the Defence, but we believe that our forces, our strengths would be much better -- put to much better use if we can address the real issues instead of going through the documents unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the daily occurrence of the Defence, complaining about documents, holding them up, not giving ERN numbers. It should be addressed in a way that the Trial Chamber has required, that is, the first port of call should be the Prosecution. Instead of taking up court time, my friend should first approach us with the ERN numbers of the documents of which he complains, and we will do our best to overcome the problem. If the documents are ones which the Prosecution does not intend to tender but rather documents which have been disclosed to the Defence under reciprocal disclosure, then if my friend cannot achieve satisfaction with the Prosecution in terms of photocopies, of course, he can inspect the document that the Prosecution possesses pursuant to Rule 66(B). Mr. President, I am reluctant to take any further time on this issue for the part of the Prosecution until my friend has spoken to us outside the sitting hours of the Trial Chamber and we see what we can achieve quietly by sitting down, looking at the documents, and trying to sort out whatever his problem is. Mr. President, there is another matter I would seek to raise briefly, when it is convenient to the Court. It is something which should take no more than five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first try to deal with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may give these documents to the usher so that they can be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when did you communicate with the Prosecution the ERN numbers that are in your determination de la defense a redaction a la problematique des pieces illisibles? When did you give these ERN numbers to the Prosecution with a request to provide you with better copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Certainly, yesterday. It was not the first time. I will check.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it seems that we have this letter from the month of July which was given to us sometime ago, or shown to us. I am not quite sure whether some of the these documents are listed there in the July letter because we did not communicate the whole history background of the case to the Prosecution. We have been checking the medical documents, however, all the time. That is not the task of the Defence, however. I think -- I am not sure, though, that in July, 2001, we pointed out that special attention should be paid to the medical documents. Perhaps some of these documents are listed therein. I did not have enough time to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...the Defence has given these numbers to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only ERN numbers I am aware of that Defence gave to us yesterday were the numbers in relation to the complaint made yesterday in court, in the Trial Chamber, yesterday afternoon, and you indicated that you wished us to pursue that issue in writing, which we would be happy to do and we are doing. I had assumed that Mr. Piletta-Zanin this morning was raising a separate issue. But again, perhaps the simple way to deal with this is for us to meet during the morning during one of the breaks and we can look at one of the documents and very quickly arrive at some sort of resolution or at least a point of understanding about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we received from the Prosecution a fax on Tuesday at 2151 hours indicating that the order of the witnesses for the week from the 10th of April onwards, and the documents listed for each of these witnesses, we responded almost immediately, that means, last night. I don't have a copy of the fax, but I personally wrote a memo that I sent personally to Mr. Ierace and it was faxed last night at around 2300 hours, which means after we received this fax we reacted immediately, and an hour after sending his fax, Mr. Ierace received all the numbers. Because as a professional courtesy, we sent him copies of the documents before sharing this with you. So they had all this last night since 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at 11 at night. This illustrates how hardworking the Defence is. And I think we should give at least a couple of hours to the Prosecution to see what they can do about it. Mr. Ierace, is there any of the numbers indicated in this letter which you would like to present before the first break?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you mean the letter that -- oh, I see, the letter that was sent on Tuesday. Do you mean whether we intend to tender any of those documents in the Tuesday letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is not a letter. It reads in French: "Determination de la defense a redaction a la problematique des pieces illisibles." That is where we find specific ERN numbers. I think it is mainly about Exhibits 3282 and 1517, and I think they are in relation with the witnesses Teslaman, Grebic and Mehonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first witness this morning is Ms. Menzilovic and none of those documents relate to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Just so I can hand a copy to Mr. Ierace. It is my original so please do not write on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is an invitation of Mr. Ierace to meet during the first break and to discuss the matter. And if you would like to give the copies already to Mr. Ierace, I think he will be glad to receive them at this very moment. So please, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the copies of the documents attached to this just to show you how difficult it is to work. Mr. Usher, please, these are the copies for the Chamber, because you will see how difficult it is to work if you don't have the appropriate data and information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand how difficult it is. I think the Chamber will be glad to look at them once the parties have met and have not been able to solve the problem as a whole or in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Usher, would you please just bring me back the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have another issue you would like to...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I indicated earlier, we proposed to call Robert Donia, an expert. We have in mind the 22nd of April. As I understand it, the following day, Tuesday the 23rd, is a day that we are not sitting. The usual rule of the cross-examination taking as long as the examination-in-chief would impact rather unfairly on the Defence if, as I anticipate, his evidence in chief is something like ten minutes, in other words, he walks into court. On the other hand, we need to have some idea of the period of cross-examination that will be allowed so that we can arrange sensibly for him to either give evidence on the 22nd or the 24th and so on, since he is travelling a consider distance to be here and the following day is not a sitting day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could the Defence inform the Chamber, say within one or two days, how much time you would need to cross-examine Mr. Donia. An expert report will be presented and briefly examined in chief, so far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be grateful if we can have that information for some stage tomorrow because of the travel arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I understand the desire of the Prosecution to be given an answer fairly quickly because, after all, it is also the desire of the Defence to be provided with information fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we will hear from you before tomorrow, if possible. Then, Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and that is Ms. Menzilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have one question, and I'm dealing with it this very moment in open court. There is a request for protective measures we discussed yesterday, and we asked some additional information to Mr. Mundis. I just remind you that we need to receive that information because --- before we can give a decision. Yes. Please proceed. Mr. Usher, would you please escort into the courtroom the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Ierace has reminded us just how important it is to be given the information promptly. I would like to ask Mr. Ierace to answer a question that is very important for the Defence and that is how and why -- how and why the documents tendered a day ago, how they were scratched out. I think that we need this answer very quickly because all the other issues pertaining to the medical documents hinge on this answer. I would like Mr. Ierace to give us a clear answer as to why all the documents that were tendered to the Chamber a few days ago, why they were, in our view, tampered with. If the Prosecution doesn't know that, perhaps they can tell us so we don't waste any more time

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that it would be better until -- unless Mr. Ierace says that he would like to respond immediately, that the Chamber will have the opportunity during the break to see what additional information we think should be given or should not be given, since the documents have not been admitted in evidence yesterday and of course we do not know what the Prosecution intends to do because we said that, without authentication, we couldn't accept them, whether there will be a moment from the Prosecution or the Defence to give any additional information in relation to that. May I just, before the witness is standing, may I just make one observation. The issue on the documents we dealt with this morning, could have dealt with in approximately half of the time easily, without losing any important aspect of the problem. Yes, so I now go and ask my --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't -- we wouldn't have wasted this time, had the documents been cleared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We all know that and we also all know this last remark took again time which was not necessary to deal with the issue. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Menzilovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, I want to apologise. You were brought into the courtroom and I didn't even say welcome, and we are still dealing with a procedural issue. I hope you will understand this. Ms. Menzilovic, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and the text of this declaration is given now to you by the usher and I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Ms. Menzilovic. The order in this court is that first questions will be put to you by counsel for the Prosecution, that is Mr. Ierace, then by counsel for the Defence, who is sitting on your left-hand side, and sometimes the Judges have additional questions as well. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Rasema Menzilovic?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you lived in Sarajevo since 1978, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married and do you have two children?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am married and I have two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war between 1992 and 1995, was your husband living with you?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your two children born in 1974 and 1980?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, did you also look after another child who was born in 1987?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that because the child's mother had died?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you live in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: In Brijesce Street and now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, the witness didn't speak out very clearly the name of the street now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the name of the street, and perhaps you could move closer to the microphones when you do so.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Brijesce in Cikma Brdo Street, number 10, and now it is the Alisma Street. It's called Alisma Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you always have electricity to your house during the war?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sometimes have to collect wood to provide fire for --

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- cooking. Where did you collect the wood?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Wherever I could find it. We would go -- we would go even further. We would go all the way to Zuc and sometimes even closer. I was also able to get something for my own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have running water to your house throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you obtain water during those years?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: From the source. It wasn't very far from there, but it was dangerous to cross the street and actually there was not -- no more water in that well or that source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war in Sarajevo, on what side of the confrontation lines did you live, in other words, on the side controlled by the Bosnian government or on the other side?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. I will make it a little simpler. During the war, was your house on the side defended by the -- or controlled by the Bosnian government or on the side controlled by the Bosnian-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: My house was exposed in the area that was under the control of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was your house, approximately, from the front line?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well I don't really know exactly, but maybe 500 metres as the crow flies. Maybe less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you mean that the Serb army was on the other side of the confrontation line from where you lived?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you ventured from your home to collect wood or water, were you ever shot at?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that when you were collecting wood?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: When I was collecting wood, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also when you were collecting water?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a preferred time to leave the house to do those things, nighttime or daytime?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What did you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tend to collect wood and water at nighttime or in daytime, in daytime?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: We would go at night and during the day as well to collect water. For the water, mainly during the night actually, but for the wood, we would also go mainly during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did those things, did you notice other people also collecting wood and water?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would always go accompanied by someone and never went alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because I wanted to have somebody with me just in case something happens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Something happened like what?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's say if I were to be wounded, so that somebody can let my children know. I was alone. I was living alone with my children. I didn't dare go alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you noticed other people also collecting wood and finding water, were they mostly men or women or children or what?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: We were mainly women. There were also men but they were older men. But they were mainly women, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see children accompanying the women?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to collect water because they were able then to help carry the water. My children also went along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was a well where you would collect water from. How far was the well from your house approximately?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but maybe 50 metres from my house, maybe more, maybe less. I am not so sure about the distance, but it was not very far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order for you to get to the well from your house, did you have to cross a road?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that road?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that it was Brijesce Brdo Cikma. That was the former name and now it is called the Bulbulistan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was the road approximately from your house?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe 20 metres from there. Not more than 25 metres. Maybe 30, but at the most. I never really measured the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I imagine that you were leaving your house and going to that well. After you crossed the road, would you continue on level ground or would you climb up or would you go down?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know what you think -- the way you mean it exactly. I didn't understand your question exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you crossed the road on the way to the well, would you then go downhill or continue on level ground, or have to climb up a hill to get to the well?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: When we would go to collect water, we would go downhill and we would have to either run or go very fast. But when we would bring the water back, we would have to go uphill and we would have to go really quickly. We would have to hurry and sometimes we even had to run.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the well to collect water, what did you take with you to put the water in?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I always carried canisters, 10-litre canisters, so two in each hand, meaning that I had 20 litres with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidently, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: January 17th, 1953.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in 1993, you were age 40; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't really count the years, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you would carry the water in two 10-litre canisters. You have also told us that on the way back to the house, initially, you would carry it uphill. Along the route between your house and the well, were there any spots which were exposed to shooting from the other side of the front line?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: From the side of the field, actually. That was the only way. From the other side, nobody ever shot at us. Nobody could see us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular area on the side of the front line controlled by the Bosnian-Serb army that you could see as you made your way along that route?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I was only able to see the field along that road. It was easy to see it clearly, but I was not able to see on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "field," what is the -- does that field have a particular name? I think I heard you say the word "polje." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: It is called "polje." It is a field. "Polje" means field in B/C/S. But we call it also Bacici, but I know it is Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you mention field, you in fact mean an area known as "polje"?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the most dangerous part of that route between your house and the well?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Further from my house, on the left-hand side, it was exposed. We always had to go between the houses. But we had to cross the road and this is where they could see us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the way back to the house, when you crossed the road, of course, you were carrying 20 litres of water; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could not move as fast, I suppose, when you were carrying the water?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Not always fast, but as fast as I could at the time, of course. I was faster than today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those years when you crossed that road coming to or from the well, were you ever with anyone who was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: The first time it happened, I went to collect water, it was also in 1991. And Haska Dudevic was also going to collect water. Her actually full name is Hasiba. And she was hit directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I think you said that was in 1991. Were there any incidents in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that Haska was wounded in 1993. That's what I saw in the month of July. That was the first event. That was the first time. And maybe I made a mistake when I said 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In that case, please continue in relation to what happened to Haska.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: She was hit in such a way that she fell down. We were also two women accompanying her and we tried to help her. She had to lie there for a long time. We couldn't bring her to the hospital right away because there was shooting, and we stayed there for a long time. We were waiting for the Civil Defence and they arrived. And she remained an invalid; she was incapacitated at 100 per cent today and it was actually the first time that I saw something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time she was shot, did you hear the sound of the shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to hear the shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what direction did you hear that sound come?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: As we went towards the water, polje was there and we could see the place called depot. I think it is still called depot today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what direction did you hear the sound of the shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Also from the direction of Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "depot" --

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: From the other side of the road. How do you want me to say it to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I always heard a sound coming from the other side of the road, from the direction of Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "depot," do you mean a train depot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never asked around to find out the exact name of that place. I know it is called the depot and also I know that the railroad tracks crossed that section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that Haska was shot, did you see any soldiers or adults carrying arms near you or near her?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in our vicinity. I never really saw that, believe me. There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was she approximately when she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really know. I think that she was born in 1948, but I am not quite certain of this so I don't really know how old she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of clothing was she wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Us women, we mainly wore a skirt. Maybe some younger women would wear trousers, but for us, we mainly wore skirts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time of day was it that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. Maybe around noon. It was very hot, that I know. For the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it raining or not raining?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. The sun was very bright that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, that was in July, 1993. When was the next time that you were with someone when they were shot when crossing that road?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: The next incident occurred while I was with Kundo Ramiza, and she was hit at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us her name again, please. I think you said "Kundo." What was her first name or what is her first name?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Ramiza Kundo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was she shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: She was shot at the beginning of November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she have containers of water with her at the time that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the sound of the shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did that sound appear to come from, which direction?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: It was always from the direction of Polje since from the other side, as I have already said, nobody could ever see us. We were always visible only from Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time of day was it that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was somewhere in the afternoon. It was the month of November. It was cold. It was a cloudy day, but we could see that -- it was also possible to see that we were women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone at all near you and her at the time that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, no, nobody else aside from the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was she wearing at that time?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: A skirt, and she had jogging pants under the skirt. She also had a sweater and a T-shirt underneath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away were you from her when she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. But I know that we always walked together close by, but I don't know at what distance I was walking from her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that you always went to the well with a friend in case you were shot. When it came time to --

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it came time for you and your friend, whoever it was, to cross the road carrying water, would you run across together or would you take turns?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Sometimes we waited. Whoever runs first was on the other side. We just really wanted to get through as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was safety on the other side when you were returning home? Was there a particular building that you could run to in order to get out of sight of the people shooting from Polje?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, crossing the road, after crossing the road, we would therefore run and there was a garage inside a house that was burnt down and there was also a very tall cherry tree, and when we ran across, we were very, very happy to get across the road and we were happy to see that we were not shot. And that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that Ramiza Kundo was shot, did you see any military weaponry or vehicles nearby?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because there were no vehicles on that road. Nobody ever took that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was she shot? What part of her body?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: She was shot in the leg. It was her left leg. And I don't know how to explain it to you. It is the muscle at the bottom of the leg. How is it called?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the calf muscle? I will withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the muscle at the bottom of the leg, under.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give her some assistance after she was wounded?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took a towel from her house. I brought it there because she was bleeding profusely, and I was trying to stop the bleeding. So I called for help. I called the Civil Defence for help and they brought her to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the next time that someone with you crossing the road with water was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: On the second time I went to collect water with the same neighbour, Hata. She is a bit older than me. But as we got to that garage, we saw that Fatima was coming back from the well. So we waited for her to cross the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Fatima's last name, or what was Fatima's last name?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Her last name is Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after Ramiza Kundo was Fatima Osmanovic shot, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: From what I can remember, it was maybe seven days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the time that Fatima Osmanovic was shot, was she returning from the well carrying water?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you cross the road with her or in front of her or were you behind her?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. We wanted to go to the well, but we didn't get there. She was coming from the well so on that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am sorry to interrupt. For the French transcript, one small comment. What seems to be on line 17 or 16 on the page in the French transcript, the name should not be written differently than what the witness said. I heard that the question was, "What is the last name of the witness" and this is not what appears in the French transcript. So this is a short comment regarding this name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proper attention will be given to it. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that you said that she and you wanted to go to the well but did not get there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Hata and myself, yes, it is true. We wanted to go to the well, but on that day we never really got to the well because Fatima was hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts on her body was she shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: She was shot in the face. Her cheek was hit and the bullet stayed near her nose, lodged in the cheek, and at the hospital they didn't dare remove it, so it stayed on her face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear a sound of the shot about the time that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: At that very moment, I am not sure but I realised that something had hit, some sort of a metallic surface, and at that very moment, she said, "I am wounded, I am injured, I am hit." And she was bleeding a lot from her nose, from her mouth, and I thought that she would die but, no, she stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war, at some stage after the war, did she die?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to that question because if something happened after the war, everything that happened after the war is outside of the scope covered by the indictment and basically it does not correspond to the chronology of the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied because the mere fact that facts are not within the period of the indictment does not always make them irrelevant. It might for example explain why she is not called as a witness, which might be of importance to know for the Chamber. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was she wearing at the time that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: She always wore a skirt, a T-shirt, a sweater. She always wore the same type of clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the weather like at that time that she was shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: It was cooler and cloudy, but it was not raining. The visibility was good. One was able to see clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know with certainty. I think it must have been around noon, but I repeat I don't know exactly what time it was. At the time, I wasn't really paying attention to time. I just hoped that I would stay alive. If I knew, for instance, that I would stay alive and that I would come here to testify before this Court, I would probably take down in writing every detail. I would note down -- I would have noted down every sound of every shell, but like this, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't expect you to have a perfect memory, Ms. Menzilovic. At the time that you were shot, did you notice whether there was anyone else near you or near her?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. If there was anyone, that would be the women, but nobody Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether there was any military equipment nearby or weaponry?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, no. I am sure about that. We were mostly civilians there. There were some elderly women but most of us were women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown P181TA, a sheet of paper which has two colour photographs on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, could I perhaps be allowed to take off my jacket? Would I be allowed to take off my jacket, as it is rather warm in here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. It is warm in here, no open windows here. Please make yourself as comfortable as possible. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, by way of explanation, the words which appear on the bottom of this sheet of paper are not part of the exhibit. The photographs were inserted into a document in the form of a report or internal document, and it is only the paragraphs which are relied upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the two photographs in front of you. Firstly, in particular, the photograph at the top. Perhaps that would be moved down the ELMO. Perhaps we can move -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am very sorry, but we cannot accept this. Even if the text has nothing to do with the photographs, we are talking about the death or the disappearance of somebody's sister. If we accept and admit this document in this form, then we need to have some sort of guidances as to whose sister it is. We don't know what this is all about. This is one way in which the information is disclosed to us, and this is not the proper way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This could have been done in a different way, without any additions to the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the three lines, the text, are not part of the exhibit. Is the Prosecution willing to take a marker pen in black and strike them out? So before the document will be tendered with the last three lines stricken out. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a copy of that exhibit which has the words removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's make that the original. And I think then the parties -- it is no necessity. I think parties and the Chamber could easily get rid of the text. But the original exhibit is now without the three last lines. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Menzilovic, do you recognise what appears in the top photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise. What I am seeing is Polje. This is the area from which they targeted us mostly with sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the photograph we can see part of a sealed road which appears to drop shortly downwards towards Polje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry, Mr. President, but I am looking at this photograph and I believe that under the photograph it says "view from the points," plural, and "impacts," plural, so we talk about a multitude of locations and points. It would be good for the Prosecution to tell us how come they have a photograph showing several points of impact except if we have a situation where a single bullet hit several places, which would be rather strange. We would like to have a clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my friend well knows the Prosecution case in relation to these incidents. Again, certainly, Ms. Pilipovic does, having attended the scene. In any event, the matter which goes to tender these documents which perhaps could be dealt with at a later stage. Put quite simply, my friend well knows that two of the scheduled incidents involve the last two incidents related to this witness, that is in relation to Ms. Kundo and Ms. Osmanovic, and that they were shot within a metre of each other. So perhaps I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on the other hand, I must say that this was not in this detail the testimony of this witness. If you are asking the witness to find the evidence of what is your case, then it might become more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us -- perhaps that last question -- I will repeat my last question to you: Towards the bottom of the photograph, we can see part of a sealed road which appears to drop sharply downwards towards Polje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of that road?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what is its name right now. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was its name then?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know what its name was at the time. Could have been Moja [phoen] Street, the street of the 1st of May. This wasn't something I was really interested in at all, the name of this road. But I can see clearly that this is indeed Polje from which we were targeted from which they opened fire on us. There were snipers there. They had a snipers' nest there. They wouldn't let us leave our houses. And I have had many sniper hits, impacts on my house, I couldn't even count them, there were so many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see in the photograph, the road where Ms. Kundo and Osmanovic were shot?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the road here, but I can't really tell you exactly but this is the road leading up to that area that populated area to that settlement. I don't know if it is Vogosca or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please point to the road on the photograph using the pointer that the usher will hand to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will you please point at the photograph, not at the screen. You will see if you point at the photograph on the right-hand side, the pointer will appear on the scene as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise really. I didn't pay attention so I didn't even see the photographs to my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicates the road on the bottom of the photograph. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that fire, that is shooting, came from Polje. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know that because I was able to see that personally since further down from my house, there was a meadow that we tilled during the night. We would see where the fire came from. You could see the shots being fired. There is a house with a four-sided roof. We saw it then. We would lie down on that field when we heard them open fire and then we would get up when the shooting stopped. Sometimes they would even shout things at us in a provocative manner, but we would be there in that field for quite a long time. So we were able to see all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that you could see the shots being fired at night. What is it exactly that you could see? What is it exactly that you could see at night?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: We were able to see the light. When the shots were fired, we could see the lights. We could see that clearly because we were lying there in that field looking at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was a house with a four-sided roof from which shots -- you could see shots being fired. You also said that you could not see that and I noticed that when you said those words, you were looking at your screen. Would you now turn to your right and look at the actual photograph. Are you able to see that house with the four-sided roof in the photograph on your right?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see it. I see the location, but I do not see the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The usher will give you a blue pen. Would you please draw a small circle to indicate the location on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: The location on the photograph? Can I make a circle? Yes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, a circle indicating where the house where the four-sided roof of the house was, yes.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see on this photograph, it seems to me that this would be the location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now look at the photograph at the bottom of the page and I think we can see a road on the left-hand side of the road are two large garbage bins. On the right-hand side of the photograph, we can see a building. Do you recognise what appears in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. You can see the point where we crossed. There was a garage here and a house, but now you can see -- there is only the house since they tore down everything and they built only the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you travelled to the well from your house, did you cross this road from the right to the left, or from the left to the right, that is, when you were going from your house to the well?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: As I went from my house to the well -- I don't know how to explain this to you. I would cross here to the left and then I would approach the water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that makes it clear which direction. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: You can see quite clearly here there was a heap of garbage here where the dumpsters are, and then the Civil Defence cleared this away and UNPROFOR also did that. On that occasion Muharem Mesanovic was wounded in the stomach also by a sniper and he was killed. They couldn't save him. I was not there at the spot but I came there later when he had already been taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what year did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well I don't really know what year it was. It may have been 1994, but I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P1812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you all right, Mrs. Menzilovic?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I look at the photographs, because I don't see very well, I have this feeling that I am -- that there is darkness. So when I look at things for a long time, I see those flashes in front of my eyes. But I will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make everything clear, Mr. President, looking at document 405 to the left, there is a signature. There is something that looks like a mechanical stamp that has been reproduced, copied badly. Perhaps it would be a good idea for Mr. Ierace to tell us, since he has the original, whether this is a badly copied stamp or is this just a trick of some sort, an optical effect, so to speak. I don't know if we have the same copies but just let us see what we with dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, am I right in understanding that, first of all, that the second page of the document is the back side which bears the name and signature, and there seems to be a kind of a rectangular shape on it. Is it just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that is the ink that came through from the front of the photograph on the original. In any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it very much seems to coincide with the markings made at the front of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is just the effect, the result of the transparency, it would be good to know whether this is a stamp or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the explanation given by Mr. Ierace is satisfactory for the moment, and if there is any other issue, we could look at the original or you inspect the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again I note, Mr. President, that if my friend had approached me before outside of court, I would have been happy to assist and save time in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look, Mrs.. Menzilovic, at the photograph in front of you and also at the sheet underneath it. If you turn to your right and look at the sheet underneath the photograph, please. Mrs.. Menzilovic, could you please turn to your right? Do you recognise on the sheet underneath, your signature and the date of the 1st of November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. I recognise my own handwriting and the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that date, did you place your signature and that date on the rear, that is, on the back of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This photograph shows a building, being a ground floor and two floors above it. Is that the same building which appears in the photograph that you looked at earlier which had -- which showed the dumper trucks or the dumpers opposite? For the record, that is --

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It is the house where we crossed, but it is the new house. The house was not there at the time because that house that was there at the time had burned down. There was a garage, too, and now there is no garage here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. Perhaps the witness could be shown P1812A very briefly so that she could compare the two buildings. That might remove any misunderstanding in the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Usher, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same building, Mrs. Menzilovic? Can you please look at the photograph at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is the same house on both photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, indeed you have told us that there was a garage and there were some building work after -- some time after these events that you've told us about. Do the black lines --

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the new house and they had taken everything else away. They had to do it, but the old building was not like this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You told us that when you were returning from the well and running across the road to safety, you knew that you had reached safety when you reached the garage. Whereabouts was the garage --

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Behind the garage. When we got behind the garage, then we would be safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that garage in relation to this photograph of the house?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: The garage would be here, and this is where we crossed. There was a large cherry tree here, and above the garage, there was the house. So that was the house that had burned down. The garage was left, but at one point it was also torn down and they repaired the whole thing. And it was quite soon after these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the transcript, the witness indicates the position of the garage to have been in the section of the house at ground level and first floor level which is not marked with black lines. The place to which they would run is the darkened area between the left-hand wall of the building and the light pole. The position of the cherry tree was slightly to the right of the light pole. Whereabouts did Mrs. Kundo live?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kundo lived right there in the house further up. Perhaps this is the house, but I think that this house here may be her house, at least, that is what I think. So she lived there. She stayed there for the entire duration of the war

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, for the transcript, the witness points to the red roof which appears immediately behind the light pole and extending behind the tree which is to the left of the light pole. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would, at this stage, normally would ask the witness be shown the CD, but given the time, perhaps I can hold that into reserve until after the morning break and go to a different topic in the meantime, to use up the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time as a whole would you still need included?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: About 10, 15 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, you first cover the other issue and then you may continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your house in relation to this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: On this photograph, when you pass through here and go behind these houses, not very far. I don't know the exact distance, but it is not far, maybe some 20 metres. I am not quite sure. But at any rate, if you go down that way and pass by these houses, you can't see it from here

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again for the transcript, the witness indicates the dark area immediately to the left of the house and then to the left of the house behind the buildings which are visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your house receive any shell fire during the war?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My house was hit by several shells and also some sniper shots, shots fired from sniper rifles, and also shots fired from anti-aircraft machine-guns. That is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the anti-aircraft fire happen in 1993? Did any of that happen in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, no. Well, fire was opened also in 1992, but at first there was a lot of shellfire in 1991 and 1992. We would spend long periods of time in our basements. We would sleep there together with the children, and also later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any shellfire, as you call it, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We came under shellfire in 1993, 1994. But I don't know when it was exactly that the shells hit my house, but they did shell us quite a lot. Also in 1992. There was a lot of intense shellfire then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any stage during the war, was there anyone -- I withdraw that. You've told us that your older child was born in 1974. Is that child a daughter?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some stage during the war, did she work for the army?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that and for how long?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I can't tell you exactly. I know that it wasn't in 1992 because that is when she graduated from the high school for electrical engineering and then she enrolled in the college, the faculty. It may have been sometime in 1993 or the beginning of 1994. But I think it was in 1993 because everybody was saying that now we can now survivor since I was in dire straits, really, at the time, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did she work for the army?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, she was demobilised and that is when she started working in her own branch. But then she studied journalism. But then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to stop you there. What were her duties when she was in the army? What was her job?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: She was in the kitchen. She would clean up a bit and she would bake bread. Help out with the food, mainly, that was her job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she ever do any fighting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry that I have to interrupt. The witness said something that was not translated. I heard her say in her language that her daughter is not working as a journalist, and that was not in the transcript. I believe that it has to be in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that there are a few dots in the transcript. Ms. Menzilovic, you told us that your daughter studied journalism and then you added something. Was that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did she work or did she not work as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now she is working in the electrical engineering branch, she is not working as a journalist. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think, in fact, Mr. President it is clear from the transcript that the pursuit of journalism happened well after the war which is why it wasn't pursued -- .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there was a part, apparently, which was not translated because -- perhaps we will stop there. It is clear now. Please proceed. If you find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us she worked in the kitchen in the army?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she the only person who lived in your household throughout the war who worked for the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and your two children and the third child born in 1987, the only people who lived in your house, in your home, during the war?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any stage work for the army or did you work for the defence of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't work for the military ever. I don't know what you mean by "the defence of Sarajevo." I only fought to survive. I wanted myself and my children to survive, to find some food because we didn't want to be forced to go begging.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That would be a convenient time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Menzilovic, we will have a break for approximately half an hour and then, for a short time, you will be examined again by counsel for the Prosecution and then you will be examined by counsel for the Defence. We will have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We returned a bit late. Apologies for that. You will hear from us about the reasons. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will update you on the meeting with the Defence after this witness is finished, if that is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us before the break, Ms. Menzilovic that you lived in the -- in your home with the three children and no one else throughout the war. Were there any military positions near your home during the war?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that your house received throughout the war shells and anti-aircraft fire. Did you also receive any small arms fire, that is, sniper-type fire?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to provide your children and yourself with more safety from sniper fire when they left the house?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: My children were leaving through the window because my entrance door was clearly seen from outside so that was our way to deal with it. And we also had a shelter in the basement at my neighbour's and during the whole war I was placing covers over the windows so that they protect me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the area held by the Bosnian Serb army, if any, could you see from your house?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First we will ask you this question: You told us earlier that your house was about 500 metres from the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the front line from your house?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the front line was that? Was that Polje or a different part?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I was unable to see Polje held by the Serbs during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that shells would land on your house. Did they damage the roof of your house?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any parts of those shells?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the first shell hit my house, that is when I saw for the first time what a shell looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any stage during the war, did you see a part of a shell which included fins or blades of metal?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was something round and there were fins around it and the inscription on the device was 82, but I don't know where they were firing from, which direction, but I did find three of those devices on my house. When the smoke would dissipate and when they would stop shooting, this is when I would go to check it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I ask you on line 24 of page 40, the transcript reads: "I was unable to see Polje help the Serbs during the war." It was not the recollection of the Chamber that that was the answer. Can you please clarify whether the transcript was correct or perhaps by repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you could see the front line from your house. What part of the front line could you see, was that Polje or a different part?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I said, and I will repeat, we were only able to see Polje. I was not able to see any other part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us that you took shelter in your neighbour's basement when your house was fired upon. Following your house being fired upon, given that shells would land on the roof. Did you discover that your roof was damaged?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly, if I discovered that it was damaged? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the shells that landed on your roof damage your roof?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The roof was completely damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to fix your roof?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to fix the roof and we tried to place some plastic covers on top. We could only work at night, however, not during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Because if they would see us, they would start shooting right away. And on two occasions when I went out to call somebody to help us fix the roof and it was very dangerous, so the neighbours would ask us, Do you need any nails? Do you need some tools? So we had to hide right away. But very often I would have to go up on the roof to put the plastic covers around 11.00 or around midnight as well. I wanted to protect the roof with the plastic covers so that when it rained, the water wouldn't drip down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were doing that at night, on any occasions, did you hear any voices from Polje, the direction of Polje?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at night, no. No. Sometimes maybe, but very rarely. The reason why I was actually allowing myself to go on top of the house was because there weren't firing, but as soon as I would hear them fire, I would not go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any occasion when from your home you could hear voices coming from the other side of the front line, people calling out and saying things?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not able. The line was closest to us, the shelling was coming from the hills. I don't know from where exactly. But with regards to snipers, they were only firing from Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstand my question. I am asking about times not when you were being sniped at, but when you were doing other things, such as fixing your roof; did you hear any calling out during those activities from the other side of the front line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the question was very clearly asked, and we can read it in line 11 or 12 so I don't think that it is necessary to repeat the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring to line 11 and 12. I am trying to -- page 43, line 11 and 12 was your observation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I am talking of page 42, page 42 and I am going to try to find the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] The question was at line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The question has in different forms been asked twice. The first occasion it could relate to the one moment when the roof was fixed; the second time the question was asked, the answer does not seem to be in a direct relationship with the question. So, therefore, Mr. Ierace you may ask the question. Perhaps you will repeat it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Menzilovic, we did not hear your answer so I will ask you the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really very sorry, Mr. President, but when I tried to search for that line, my computer broke down again so I would like to ask the assistance of a technician, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could someone assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Yes, I see Madam Registrar is taking the necessary measures. Mr. Ierace, perhaps it would be wise to repeat the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Menzilovic, when you were fixing your roof, did you hear any calling out, apparently to you, from the other side of the front line?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that they were calling out from Polje, but on the other side nobody could have seen me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that they couldn't have seen you. What did they say? What did the voice or voices say?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: We needed to nail down a piece of wood to nail down the plastic cover. I would hear them say, "Do you need any nails?" And on two occasions, as I said, during the war when I would go up on the roof I would hear them say that. So quite probably they were mocking us, probably. We were not even able to show our faces. We would only stick our head out. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On other occasions, did you hear voices coming from the other side of the front line saying other things to you?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given that you were fixing the roof at night, how do you think that they were able to know what you were doing, that is, fixing your roof?

utterances.speaker: RASEMA MENZILOVIC
